  16 │ **Please refer to the** `tenacity documentation <https://tenacity.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>`_ **for a better experience.**
  17 │ 
  18 │ Tenacity is an Apache 2.0 licensed general-purpose retrying library, written in
  19 │ Python, to simplify the task of adding retry behavior to just about anything.
  20 │ It originates from `a fork of retrying
  21 │ <https://github.com/rholder/retrying/issues/65>`_ which is sadly no longer
  22 │ `maintained <https://julien.danjou.info/python-tenacity/>`_. Tenacity isn't
  23 │ api compatible with retrying but adds significant new functionality and
  24 │ fixes a number of longstanding bugs.
  25 │ 
  26 │ The simplest use case is retrying a flaky function whenever an `Exception`
  27 │ occurs until a value is returned.
  28 │ 
  29 │ .. testcode::
  30 │ 
  31 │     import random
  32 │     from tenacity import retry
  33 │ 
  34 │     @retry
  35 │     def do_something_unreliable():
  36 │         if random.randint(0, 10) > 1:
  37 │             raise IOError("Broken sauce, everything is hosed!!!111one")
  38 │         else:
  39 │             return "Awesome sauce!"
  40 │ 
  41 │     print(do_something_unreliable())
  42 │

  57 │ Features
  58 │ --------
  59 │ 
  60 │ - Generic Decorator API
  61 │ - Specify stop condition (i.e. limit by number of attempts)
  62 │ - Specify wait condition (i.e. exponential backoff sleeping between attempts)
  63 │ - Customize retrying on Exceptions
  64 │ - Customize retrying on expected returned result
  65 │ - Retry on coroutines
  66 │ - Retry code block with context manager
  67 │ 
  68 │ 
  69 │ Installation
  70 │ ------------
  71 │ 
  72 │ To install *tenacity*, simply:
  73 │ 
  74 │ .. code-block:: bash
  75 │ 
  76 │     $ pip install tenacity
  77 │ 
  78 │ 
  79 │ Examples
  80 │ ----------
  81 │ 
  82 │ Basic Retry
  83 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~
  84 │ 
  85 │ .. testsetup::
  86 │ 
  87 │     import logging
  88 │     #
  89 │     # Note the following import is used for demonstration convenience only.
  90 │     # Production code should always explicitly import the names it needs.
  91 │     #
  92 │     from tenacity import *
  93 │ 
  94 │     class MyException(Exception):
  95 │         pass
  96 │ 
  97 │ As you saw above, the default behavior is to retry forever without waiting when
  98 │ an exception is raised.
  99 │ 
 100 │ .. testcode::
 101 │ 
 102 │     @retry
 103 │     def never_gonna_give_you_up():
 104 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions, don't wait between retries")
 105 │         raise Exception
 106 │ 
 107 │ Stopping
 108 │ ~~~~~~~~
 109 │ 
 110 │ Let's be a little less persistent and set some boundaries, such as the number
 111 │ of attempts before giving up.
 112 │ 
 113 │ .. testcode::
 114 │ 
 115 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(7))
 116 │     def stop_after_7_attempts():
 117 │         print("Stopping after 7 attempts")
 118 │         raise Exception
 119 │ 
 120 │ We don't have all day, so let's set a boundary for how long we should be
 121 │ retrying stuff.
 122 │ 
 123 │ .. testcode::
 124 │ 
 125 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_delay(10))
 126 │     def stop_after_10_s():
 127 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds")
 128 │         raise Exception
 129 │ 
 130 │ If you're on a tight deadline, and exceeding your delay time isn't ok,
 131 │ then you can give up on retries one attempt before you would exceed the delay.
 132 │ 
 133 │ .. testcode::
 134 │ 
 135 │     @retry(stop=stop_before_delay(10))
 136 │     def stop_before_10_s():
 137 │         print("Stopping 1 attempt before 10 seconds")
 138 │         raise Exception
 139 │ 
 140 │ You can combine several stop conditions by using the `|` operator:
 141 │ 
 142 │ .. testcode::
 143 │ 
 144 │     @retry(stop=(stop_after_delay(10) | stop_after_attempt(5)))
 145 │     def stop_after_10_s_or_5_retries():
 146 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds or 5 retries")
 147 │         raise Exception
 148 │ 
 149 │ Waiting before retrying
 150 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 151 │ 
 152 │ Most things don't like to be polled as fast as possible, so let's just wait 2
 153 │ seconds between retries.
 154 │ 
 155 │ .. testcode::
 156 │ 
 157 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(2))
 158 │     def wait_2_s():
 159 │         print("Wait 2 second between retries")
 160 │         raise Exception
 161 │ 
 162 │ Some things perform best with a bit of randomness injected.
 163 │ 
 164 │ .. testcode::
 165 │ 
 166 │     @retry(wait=wait_random(min=1, max=2))
 167 │     def wait_random_1_to_2_s():
 168 │         print("Randomly wait 1 to 2 seconds between retries")
 169 │         raise Exception
 170 │ 
 171 │ Then again, it's hard to beat exponential backoff when retrying distributed
 172 │ services and other remote endpoints.
 173 │ 
 174 │ .. testcode::
 175 │ 
 176 │     @retry(wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=4, max=10))
 177 │     def wait_exponential_1():
 178 │         print("Wait 2^x * 1 second between each retry starting with 4 seconds, then up to 10 seconds, then 10 seconds afterwards")
 179 │         raise Exception
 180 │ 
 181 │ 
 182 │ Then again, it's also hard to beat combining fixed waits and jitter (to
 183 │ help avoid thundering herds) when retrying distributed services and other
 184 │ remote endpoints.
 185 │ 
 186 │ .. testcode::
 187 │ 
 188 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(3) + wait_random(0, 2))
 189 │     def wait_fixed_jitter():
 190 │         print("Wait at least 3 seconds, and add up to 2 seconds of random delay")
 191 │         raise Exception
 192 │ 
 193 │ When multiple processes are in contention for a shared resource, exponentially
 194 │ increasing jitter helps minimise collisions.
 195 │ 
 196 │ .. testcode::
 197 │ 
 198 │     @retry(wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=1, max=60))
 199 │     def wait_exponential_jitter():
 200 │         print("Randomly wait up to 2^x * 1 seconds between each retry until the range reaches 60 seconds, then randomly up to 60 seconds afterwards")
 201 │         raise Exception
 202 │ 
 203 │ 
 204 │ Sometimes it's necessary to build a chain of backoffs.
 205 │ 
 206 │ .. testcode::
 207 │ 
 208 │     @retry(wait=wait_chain(*[wait_fixed(3) for i in range(3)] +
 209 │                            [wait_fixed(7) for i in range(2)] +
 210 │                            [wait_fixed(9)]))
 211 │     def wait_fixed_chained():
 212 │         print("Wait 3s for 3 attempts, 7s for the next 2 attempts and 9s for all attempts thereafter")
 213 │         raise Exception
 214 │ 
 215 │ Whether to retry
 216 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 217 │ 
 218 │ We have a few options for dealing with retries that raise specific or general
 219 │ exceptions, as in the cases here.
 220 │ 
 221 │ .. testcode::
 222 │ 
 223 │     class ClientError(Exception):
 224 │         """Some type of client error."""
 225 │ 
 226 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(IOError))
 227 │     def might_io_error():
 228 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if an IOError occurs, raise any other errors")
 229 │         raise Exception
 230 │ 
 231 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_not_exception_type(ClientError))
 232 │     def might_client_error():
 233 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if any error other than ClientError occurs. Immediately raise ClientError.")
 234 │         raise Exception
 235 │ 
 236 │ We can also use the result of the function to alter the behavior of retrying.
 237 │ 
 238 │ .. testcode::
 239 │ 
 240 │     def is_none_p(value):
 241 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 242 │         return value is None
 243 │ 
 244 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_result(is_none_p))
 245 │     def might_return_none():
 246 │         print("Retry with no wait if return value is None")
 247 │ 
 248 │ See also these methods:
 249 │ 
 250 │ .. testcode::
 251 │ 
 252 │     retry_if_exception
 253 │     retry_if_exception_type
 254 │     retry_if_not_exception_type
 255 │     retry_unless_exception_type
 256 │     retry_if_result
 257 │     retry_if_not_result
 258 │     retry_if_exception_message
 259 │     retry_if_not_exception_message
 260 │     retry_any
 261 │     retry_all
 262 │ 
 263 │ We can also combine several conditions:
 264 │ 
 265 │ .. testcode::
 266 │ 
 267 │     def is_none_p(value):
 268 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 269 │         return value is None
 270 │ 
 271 │     @retry(retry=(retry_if_result(is_none_p) | retry_if_exception_type()))
 272 │     def might_return_none():
 273 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions with no wait if return value is None")
 274 │ 
 275 │ Any combination of stop, wait, etc. is also supported to give you the freedom
 276 │ to mix and match.
 277 │ 
 278 │ It's also possible to retry explicitly at any time by raising the `TryAgain`
 279 │ exception:
 280 │ 
 281 │ .. testcode::
 282 │ 
 283 │    @retry
 284 │    def do_something():
 285 │        result = something_else()
 286 │        if result == 23:
 287 │           raise TryAgain
 288 │ 
 289 │ Error Handling
 290 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 291 │ 
 292 │ Normally when your function fails its final time (and will not be retried again based on your settings),
 293 │ a `RetryError` is raised. The exception your code encountered will be shown somewhere in the *middle*
 294 │ of the stack trace.
 295 │ 
 296 │ If you would rather see the exception your code encountered at the *end* of the stack trace (where it
 297 │ is most visible), you can set `reraise=True`.
 298 │ 
 299 │ .. testcode::
 300 │ 
 301 │     @retry(reraise=True, stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 302 │     def raise_my_exception():
 303 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 304 │ 
 305 │     try:
 306 │         raise_my_exception()
 307 │     except MyException:
 308 │         # timed out retrying
 309 │         pass
 310 │ 
 311 │ Before and After Retry, and Logging
 312 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 313 │ 
 314 │ It's possible to execute an action before any attempt of calling the function
 315 │ by using the before callback function:
 316 │ 
 317 │ .. testcode::
 318 │ 
 319 │     import logging
 320 │     import sys
 321 │ 
 322 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 323 │ 
 324 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 325 │ 
 326 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before=before_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 327 │     def raise_my_exception():
 328 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 329 │ 
 330 │ In the same spirit, It's possible to execute after a call that failed:
 331 │ 
 332 │ .. testcode::
 333 │ 
 334 │     import logging
 335 │     import sys
 336 │ 
 337 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 338 │ 
 339 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 340 │ 
 341 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=after_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 342 │     def raise_my_exception():
 343 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 344 │ 
 345 │ It's also possible to only log failures that are going to be retried. Normally
 346 │ retries happen after a wait interval, so the keyword argument is called
 347 │ ``before_sleep``:
 348 │ 
 349 │ .. testcode::
 350 │ 
 351 │     import logging
 352 │     import sys
 353 │ 
 354 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 355 │ 
 356 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 357 │ 
 358 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 359 │            before_sleep=before_sleep_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 360 │     def raise_my_exception():
 361 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 362 │ 
 363 │ 
 364 │ Statistics
 365 │ ~~~~~~~~~~
 366 │ 
 367 │ You can access the statistics about the retry made over a function by using the
 368 │ `statistics` attribute attached to the function:
 369 │ 
 370 │ .. testcode::
 371 │ 
 372 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 373 │     def raise_my_exception():
 374 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 375 │ 
 376 │     try:
 377 │         raise_my_exception()
 378 │     except Exception:
 379 │         pass
 380 │ 
 381 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)
 382 │

 385 │ 
 386 │    ...

 388 │ Custom Callbacks
 389 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 390 │ 
 391 │ You can also define your own callbacks. The callback should accept one
 392 │ parameter called ``retry_state`` that contains all information about current
 393 │ retry invocation.
 394 │ 
 395 │ For example, you can call a custom callback function after all retries failed,
 396 │ without raising an exception (or you can re-raise or do anything really)
 397 │ 
 398 │ .. testcode::
 399 │ 
 400 │     def return_last_value(retry_state):
 401 │         """return the result of the last call attempt"""
 402 │         return retry_state.outcome.result()
 403 │ 
 404 │     def is_false(value):
 405 │         """Return True if value is False"""
 406 │         return value is False
 407 │ 
 408 │     # will return False after trying 3 times to get a different result
 409 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 410 │            retry_error_callback=return_last_value,
 411 │            retry=retry_if_result(is_false))
 412 │     def eventually_return_false():
 413 │         return False
 414 │ 
 415 │ RetryCallState
 416 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 417 │ 
 418 │ ``retry_state`` argument is an object of :class:`~tenacity.RetryCallState` class.
 419 │ Its most useful attributes are:
 420 │ 
 421 │ * ``attempt_number`` — number of the current attempt (starts at 1)
 422 │ * ``outcome`` — a :class:`concurrent.futures.Future` holding the last result or exception
 423 │ * ``seconds_since_start`` — total elapsed seconds from the first attempt to the last outcome (``None`` if no outcome yet)
 424 │ * ``idle_for`` — cumulative seconds spent sleeping between attempts
 425 │ * ``start_time`` — :func:`time.monotonic` timestamp of the first attempt
 426 │ 
 427 │ For example, to log the total elapsed time after all retries:
 428 │ 
 429 │ .. testcode::
 430 │ 
 431 │     import logging
 432 │ 
 433 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 434 │ 
 435 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 436 │ 
 437 │     def log_elapsed(retry_state):
 438 │         logger.info('Finished after %.3fs', retry_state.seconds_since_start)
 439 │ 
 440 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=log_elapsed)
 441 │     def raise_my_exception():
 442 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 443 │ 
 444 │     try:
 445 │         raise_my_exception()
 446 │     except RetryError:
 447 │         pass
 448 │ 
 449 │ Other Custom Callbacks
 450 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 451 │ 
 452 │ It's also possible to define custom callbacks for other keyword arguments.
 453 │ 
 454 │ .. function:: my_stop(retry_state)
 455 │ 
 456 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 457 │    :return: whether or not retrying should stop
 458 │    :rtype: bool
 459 │ 
 460 │ .. function:: my_wait(retry_state)
 461 │ 
 462 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 463 │    :return: number of seconds to wait before next retry
 464 │    :rtype: float
 465 │ 
 466 │ .. function:: my_retry(retry_state)
 467 │ 
 468 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 469 │    :return: whether or not retrying should continue
 470 │    :rtype: bool
 471 │ 
 472 │ .. function:: my_before(retry_state)
 473 │ 
 474 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 475 │ 
 476 │ .. function:: my_after(retry_state)
 477 │ 
 478 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 479 │ 
 480 │ .. function:: my_before_sleep(retry_state)
 481 │ 
 482 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 483 │ 
 484 │ Here's an example with a custom ``before_sleep`` function:
 485 │ 
 486 │ .. testcode::
 487 │ 
 488 │     import logging
 489 │ 
 490 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 491 │ 
 492 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 493 │ 
 494 │     def my_before_sleep(retry_state):
 495 │         if retry_state.attempt_number < 1:
 496 │             loglevel = logging.INFO
 497 │         else:
 498 │             loglevel = logging.WARNING
 499 │         logger.log(
 500 │             loglevel, 'Retrying %s: attempt %s ended with: %s',
 501 │             retry_state.fn, retry_state.attempt_number, retry_state.outcome)
 502 │ 
 503 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before_sleep=my_before_sleep)
 504 │     def raise_my_exception():
 505 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 506 │ 
 507 │     try:
 508 │         raise_my_exception()
 509 │     except RetryError:
 510 │         pass
 511 │ 
 512 │ 
 513 │ Common Patterns
 514 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 515 │ 
 516 │ **Running setup code between retries** (e.g. reconnecting):
 517 │ 
 518 │ .. testcode::
 519 │ 
 520 │     def reconnect(retry_state):
 521 │         print("Reconnecting before next attempt...")
 522 │ 
 523 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before_sleep=reconnect)
 524 │     def send_data():
 525 │         raise MyException("connection lost")
 526 │ 
 527 │     try:
 528 │         send_data()
 529 │     except RetryError:
 530 │         pass
 531 │ 
 532 │ .. testoutput::
 533 │    :hide:
 534 │ 
 535 │    ...
 536 │ 
 537 │ The ``before_sleep`` callback runs after a failed attempt and before sleeping,
 538 │ making it ideal for re-establishing connections, refreshing tokens, or any
 539 │ other setup that needs to happen before the next attempt.
 540 │ 
 541 │ **Accessing the attempt number inside the function** using the iterator API:
 542 │ 
 543 │ .. testcode::
 544 │ 
 545 │     from tenacity import Retrying
 546 │ 
 547 │     for attempt in Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 548 │         with attempt:
 549 │             print(f"Attempt {attempt.retry_state.attempt_number}")
 550 │             if attempt.retry_state.attempt_number < 3:
 551 │                 raise MyException("not yet")
 552 │

 554 │    :hide:
 555 │ 
 556 │    ...

 559 │ Changing Arguments at Run Time
 560 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 561 │ 
 562 │ You can change the arguments of a retry decorator as needed when calling it by
 563 │ using the `retry_with` function attached to the wrapped function:
 564 │ 
 565 │ .. testcode::
 566 │ 
 567 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 568 │     def raise_my_exception():
 569 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 570 │ 
 571 │     try:
 572 │         raise_my_exception.retry_with(stop=stop_after_attempt(4))()
 573 │     except Exception:
 574 │         pass
 575 │ 
 576 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)
 577 │ 
 578 │ .. testoutput::
 579 │    :hide:
 580 │ 
 581 │    ...
 582 │ 
 583 │ If you want to use variables to set up the retry parameters, you don't have
 584 │ to use the `retry` decorator - you can instead use `Retrying` directly:
 585 │ 
 586 │ .. testcode::
 587 │ 
 588 │     def never_good_enough(arg1):
 589 │         raise Exception('Invalid argument: {}'.format(arg1))
 590 │ 
 591 │     def try_never_good_enough(max_attempts=3):
 592 │         retryer = Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(max_attempts), reraise=True)
 593 │         retryer(never_good_enough, 'I really do try')
 594 │ 
 595 │ You may also want to change the behaviour of a decorated function temporarily,
 596 │ like in tests to avoid unnecessary wait times. You can modify/patch the `retry`
 597 │ attribute attached to the function. Bear in mind this is a write-only attribute,
 598 │ statistics should be read from the function `statistics` attribute.
 599 │ 
 600 │ .. testcode::
 601 │ 
 602 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_fixed(3))
 603 │     def raise_my_exception():
 604 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 605 │ 
 606 │     from unittest import mock
 607 │ 
 608 │     with mock.patch.object(raise_my_exception.retry, "wait", wait_fixed(0)):
 609 │         try:
 610 │             raise_my_exception()
 611 │         except Exception:
 612 │             pass
 613 │ 
 614 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)
 615 │

 617 │    :hide:
 618 │ 
 619 │    ...

 621 │ Retrying code block
 622 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 623 │ 
 624 │ Tenacity allows you to retry a code block without the need to wraps it in an
 625 │ isolated function. This makes it easy to isolate failing block while sharing
 626 │ context. The trick is to combine a for loop and a context manager.
 627 │ 
 628 │ .. testcode::
 629 │ 
 630 │    from tenacity import Retrying, RetryError, stop_after_attempt
 631 │ 
 632 │    try:
 633 │        for attempt in Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 634 │            with attempt:
 635 │                raise Exception('My code is failing!')
 636 │    except RetryError:
 637 │        pass
 638 │ 
 639 │ You can configure every details of retry policy by configuring the Retrying
 640 │ object.
 641 │ 
 642 │ With async code you can use AsyncRetrying.
 643 │ 
 644 │ .. testcode::
 645 │ 
 646 │    from tenacity import AsyncRetrying, RetryError, stop_after_attempt
 647 │ 
 648 │    async def function():
 649 │       try:
 650 │           async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 651 │               with attempt:
 652 │                   raise Exception('My code is failing!')
 653 │       except RetryError:
 654 │           pass
 655 │ 
 656 │ In both cases, you may want to set the result to the attempt so it's available
 657 │ in retry strategies like ``retry_if_result``. This can be done accessing the
 658 │ ``retry_state`` property:
 659 │ 
 660 │ .. testcode::
 661 │ 
 662 │     from tenacity import AsyncRetrying, retry_if_result
 663 │ 
 664 │     async def function():
 665 │        async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(retry=retry_if_result(lambda x: x < 3)):
 666 │            with attempt:
 667 │                result = 1  # Some complex calculation, function call, etc.
 668 │            if not attempt.retry_state.outcome.failed:
 669 │                attempt.retry_state.set_result(result)
 670 │        return result
 671 │ 
 672 │ Async and retry
 673 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 674 │ 
 675 │ Finally, ``retry`` works also on asyncio, Trio, and Tornado coroutines.
 676 │ Sleeps are done asynchronously too.
 677 │ 
 678 │ .. code-block:: python
 679 │ 
 680 │     @retry
 681 │     async def my_asyncio_function():
 682 │         await asyncio.getaddrinfo('8.8.8.8', 53)
 683 │ 
 684 │ .. code-block:: python
 685 │ 
 686 │     @retry
 687 │     async def my_async_trio_function():
 688 │         await trio.socket.getaddrinfo('8.8.8.8', 53)
 689 │ 
 690 │ .. code-block:: python
 691 │ 
 692 │     @retry
 693 │     async def my_async_tornado_function(http_client, url):
 694 │         await http_client.fetch(url)
 695 │ 
 696 │ You can use alternative event loops by passing the correct sleep function:
 697 │ 
 698 │ .. code-block:: python
 699 │ 
 700 │     @retry(sleep=trio.sleep)
 701 │     async def my_async_trio_function_with_sleep():
 702 │         ...

  16 │ **Please refer to the** `tenacity documentation <https://tenacity.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>`_ **for a better experience.**
  17 │ 
  18 │ Tenacity is an Apache 2.0 licensed general-purpose retrying library, written in
  19 │ Python, to simplify the task of adding retry behavior to just about anything.
  20 │ It originates from `a fork of retrying
  21 │ <https://github.com/rholder/retrying/issues/65>`_ which is sadly no longer
  22 │ `maintained <https://julien.danjou.info/python-tenacity/>`_. Tenacity isn't
  23 │ api compatible with retrying but adds significant new functionality and
  24 │ fixes a number of longstanding bugs.
  25 │ 
  26 │ The simplest use case is retrying a flaky function whenever an `Exception`
  27 │ occurs until a value is returned.
  28 │ 
  29 │ .. testcode::
  30 │ 
  31 │     import random
  32 │     from tenacity import retry
  33 │ 
  34 │     @retry
  35 │     def do_something_unreliable():
  36 │         if random.randint(0, 10) > 1:
  37 │             raise IOError("Broken sauce, everything is hosed!!!111one")
  38 │         else:
  39 │             return "Awesome sauce!"
  40 │ 
  41 │     print(do_something_unreliable())
  42 │ 
  43 │ .. testoutput::
  44 │    :hide:
  45 │ 
  46 │    Awesome sauce!

  57 │ Features
  58 │ --------
  59 │ 
  60 │ - Generic Decorator API
  61 │ - Specify stop condition (i.e. limit by number of attempts)
  62 │ - Specify wait condition (i.e. exponential backoff sleeping between attempts)
  63 │ - Customize retrying on Exceptions
  64 │ - Customize retrying on expected returned result
  65 │ - Retry on coroutines
  66 │ - Retry code block with context manager

  79 │ Examples
  80 │ ----------
  81 │ 
  82 │ Basic Retry
  83 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~
  84 │ 
  85 │ .. testsetup::
  86 │ 
  87 │     import logging
  88 │     #
  89 │     # Note the following import is used for demonstration convenience only.
  90 │     # Production code should always explicitly import the names it needs.
  91 │     #
  92 │     from tenacity import *
  93 │ 
  94 │     class MyException(Exception):
  95 │         pass
  96 │ 
  97 │ As you saw above, the default behavior is to retry forever without waiting when
  98 │ an exception is raised.
  99 │ 
 100 │ .. testcode::
 101 │ 
 102 │     @retry
 103 │     def never_gonna_give_you_up():
 104 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions, don't wait between retries")
 105 │         raise Exception
 106 │ 
 107 │ Stopping
 108 │ ~~~~~~~~
 109 │ 
 110 │ Let's be a little less persistent and set some boundaries, such as the number
 111 │ of attempts before giving up.
 112 │ 
 113 │ .. testcode::
 114 │ 
 115 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(7))
 116 │     def stop_after_7_attempts():
 117 │         print("Stopping after 7 attempts")
 118 │         raise Exception
 119 │ 
 120 │ We don't have all day, so let's set a boundary for how long we should be
 121 │ retrying stuff.
 122 │ 
 123 │ .. testcode::
 124 │ 
 125 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_delay(10))
 126 │     def stop_after_10_s():
 127 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds")
 128 │         raise Exception
 129 │ 
 130 │ If you're on a tight deadline, and exceeding your delay time isn't ok,
 131 │ then you can give up on retries one attempt before you would exceed the delay.
 132 │ 
 133 │ .. testcode::
 134 │ 
 135 │     @retry(stop=stop_before_delay(10))
 136 │     def stop_before_10_s():
 137 │         print("Stopping 1 attempt before 10 seconds")
 138 │         raise Exception
 139 │ 
 140 │ You can combine several stop conditions by using the `|` operator:
 141 │ 
 142 │ .. testcode::
 143 │ 
 144 │     @retry(stop=(stop_after_delay(10) | stop_after_attempt(5)))
 145 │     def stop_after_10_s_or_5_retries():
 146 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds or 5 retries")
 147 │         raise Exception
 148 │ 
 149 │ Waiting before retrying
 150 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 151 │ 
 152 │ Most things don't like to be polled as fast as possible, so let's just wait 2
 153 │ seconds between retries.
 154 │ 
 155 │ .. testcode::
 156 │ 
 157 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(2))
 158 │     def wait_2_s():
 159 │         print("Wait 2 second between retries")
 160 │         raise Exception
 161 │ 
 162 │ Some things perform best with a bit of randomness injected.
 163 │ 
 164 │ .. testcode::
 165 │ 
 166 │     @retry(wait=wait_random(min=1, max=2))
 167 │     def wait_random_1_to_2_s():
 168 │         print("Randomly wait 1 to 2 seconds between retries")
 169 │         raise Exception
 170 │ 
 171 │ Then again, it's hard to beat exponential backoff when retrying distributed
 172 │ services and other remote endpoints.
 173 │ 
 174 │ .. testcode::
 175 │ 
 176 │     @retry(wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=4, max=10))
 177 │     def wait_exponential_1():
 178 │         print("Wait 2^x * 1 second between each retry starting with 4 seconds, then up to 10 seconds, then 10 seconds afterwards")
 179 │         raise Exception
 180 │ 
 181 │ 
 182 │ Then again, it's also hard to beat combining fixed waits and jitter (to
 183 │ help avoid thundering herds) when retrying distributed services and other
 184 │ remote endpoints.
 185 │ 
 186 │ .. testcode::
 187 │ 
 188 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(3) + wait_random(0, 2))
 189 │     def wait_fixed_jitter():
 190 │         print("Wait at least 3 seconds, and add up to 2 seconds of random delay")
 191 │         raise Exception
 192 │ 
 193 │ When multiple processes are in contention for a shared resource, exponentially
 194 │ increasing jitter helps minimise collisions.
 195 │ 
 196 │ .. testcode::
 197 │ 
 198 │     @retry(wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=1, max=60))
 199 │     def wait_exponential_jitter():
 200 │         print("Randomly wait up to 2^x * 1 seconds between each retry until the range reaches 60 seconds, then randomly up to 60 seconds afterwards")
 201 │         raise Exception
 202 │ 
 203 │ 
 204 │ Sometimes it's necessary to build a chain of backoffs.
 205 │ 
 206 │ .. testcode::
 207 │ 
 208 │     @retry(wait=wait_chain(*[wait_fixed(3) for i in range(3)] +
 209 │                            [wait_fixed(7) for i in range(2)] +
 210 │                            [wait_fixed(9)]))
 211 │     def wait_fixed_chained():
 212 │         print("Wait 3s for 3 attempts, 7s for the next 2 attempts and 9s for all attempts thereafter")
 213 │         raise Exception

 215 │ Whether to retry
 216 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 217 │ 
 218 │ We have a few options for dealing with retries that raise specific or general
 219 │ exceptions, as in the cases here.
 220 │ 
 221 │ .. testcode::
 222 │ 
 223 │     class ClientError(Exception):
 224 │         """Some type of client error."""
 225 │ 
 226 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(IOError))
 227 │     def might_io_error():
 228 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if an IOError occurs, raise any other errors")
 229 │         raise Exception
 230 │ 
 231 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_not_exception_type(ClientError))
 232 │     def might_client_error():
 233 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if any error other than ClientError occurs. Immediately raise ClientError.")
 234 │         raise Exception
 235 │ 
 236 │ We can also use the result of the function to alter the behavior of retrying.
 237 │ 
 238 │ .. testcode::
 239 │ 
 240 │     def is_none_p(value):
 241 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 242 │         return value is None
 243 │ 
 244 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_result(is_none_p))
 245 │     def might_return_none():
 246 │         print("Retry with no wait if return value is None")
 247 │ 
 248 │ See also these methods:
 249 │ 
 250 │ .. testcode::
 251 │ 
 252 │     retry_if_exception
 253 │     retry_if_exception_type
 254 │     retry_if_not_exception_type
 255 │     retry_unless_exception_type
 256 │     retry_if_result
 257 │     retry_if_not_result
 258 │     retry_if_exception_message
 259 │     retry_if_not_exception_message
 260 │     retry_any
 261 │     retry_all
 262 │ 
 263 │ We can also combine several conditions:
 264 │ 
 265 │ .. testcode::
 266 │ 
 267 │     def is_none_p(value):
 268 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 269 │         return value is None
 270 │ 
 271 │     @retry(retry=(retry_if_result(is_none_p) | retry_if_exception_type()))
 272 │     def might_return_none():
 273 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions with no wait if return value is None")
 274 │ 
 275 │ Any combination of stop, wait, etc. is also supported to give you the freedom
 276 │ to mix and match.
 277 │ 
 278 │ It's also possible to retry explicitly at any time by raising the `TryAgain`
 279 │ exception:
 280 │ 
 281 │ .. testcode::
 282 │ 
 283 │    @retry
 284 │    def do_something():
 285 │        result = something_else()
 286 │        if result == 23:
 287 │           raise TryAgain

 289 │ Error Handling
 290 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 291 │ 
 292 │ Normally when your function fails its final time (and will not be retried again based on your settings),
 293 │ a `RetryError` is raised. The exception your code encountered will be shown somewhere in the *middle*
 294 │ of the stack trace.
 295 │ 
 296 │ If you would rather see the exception your code encountered at the *end* of the stack trace (where it
 297 │ is most visible), you can set `reraise=True`.
 298 │ 
 299 │ .. testcode::
 300 │ 
 301 │     @retry(reraise=True, stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 302 │     def raise_my_exception():
 303 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 304 │ 
 305 │     try:
 306 │         raise_my_exception()
 307 │     except MyException:
 308 │         # timed out retrying
 309 │         pass

 311 │ Before and After Retry, and Logging
 312 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 313 │ 
 314 │ It's possible to execute an action before any attempt of calling the function
 315 │ by using the before callback function:
 316 │ 
 317 │ .. testcode::
 318 │ 
 319 │     import logging
 320 │     import sys
 321 │ 
 322 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 323 │ 
 324 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 325 │ 
 326 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before=before_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 327 │     def raise_my_exception():
 328 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 329 │ 
 330 │ In the same spirit, It's possible to execute after a call that failed:
 331 │ 
 332 │ .. testcode::
 333 │ 
 334 │     import logging
 335 │     import sys
 336 │ 
 337 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 338 │ 
 339 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 340 │ 
 341 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=after_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 342 │     def raise_my_exception():
 343 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 344 │ 
 345 │ It's also possible to only log failures that are going to be retried. Normally
 346 │ retries happen after a wait interval, so the keyword argument is called
 347 │ ``before_sleep``:
 348 │ 
 349 │ .. testcode::
 350 │ 
 351 │     import logging
 352 │     import sys
 353 │ 
 354 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 355 │ 
 356 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 357 │ 
 358 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 359 │            before_sleep=before_sleep_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 360 │     def raise_my_exception():
 361 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 362 │

 388 │ Custom Callbacks
 389 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 390 │ 
 391 │ You can also define your own callbacks. The callback should accept one
 392 │ parameter called ``retry_state`` that contains all information about current
 393 │ retry invocation.
 394 │ 
 395 │ For example, you can call a custom callback function after all retries failed,
 396 │ without raising an exception (or you can re-raise or do anything really)
 397 │ 
 398 │ .. testcode::
 399 │ 
 400 │     def return_last_value(retry_state):
 401 │         """return the result of the last call attempt"""
 402 │         return retry_state.outcome.result()
 403 │ 
 404 │     def is_false(value):
 405 │         """Return True if value is False"""
 406 │         return value is False
 407 │ 
 408 │     # will return False after trying 3 times to get a different result
 409 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 410 │            retry_error_callback=return_last_value,
 411 │            retry=retry_if_result(is_false))
 412 │     def eventually_return_false():
 413 │         return False
 414 │ 
 415 │ RetryCallState
 416 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 417 │ 
 418 │ ``retry_state`` argument is an object of :class:`~tenacity.RetryCallState` class.
 419 │ Its most useful attributes are:
 420 │ 
 421 │ * ``attempt_number`` — number of the current attempt (starts at 1)
 422 │ * ``outcome`` — a :class:`concurrent.futures.Future` holding the last result or exception
 423 │ * ``seconds_since_start`` — total elapsed seconds from the first attempt to the last outcome (``None`` if no outcome yet)
 424 │ * ``idle_for`` — cumulative seconds spent sleeping between attempts
 425 │ * ``start_time`` — :func:`time.monotonic` timestamp of the first attempt
 426 │ 
 427 │ For example, to log the total elapsed time after all retries:
 428 │ 
 429 │ .. testcode::
 430 │ 
 431 │     import logging
 432 │ 
 433 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 434 │ 
 435 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 436 │ 
 437 │     def log_elapsed(retry_state):
 438 │         logger.info('Finished after %.3fs', retry_state.seconds_since_start)
 439 │ 
 440 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=log_elapsed)
 441 │     def raise_my_exception():
 442 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 443 │ 
 444 │     try:
 445 │         raise_my_exception()
 446 │     except RetryError:
 447 │         pass

 449 │ Other Custom Callbacks
 450 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 451 │ 
 452 │ It's also possible to define custom callbacks for other keyword arguments.
 453 │ 
 454 │ .. function:: my_stop(retry_state)
 455 │ 
 456 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 457 │    :return: whether or not retrying should stop
 458 │    :rtype: bool
 459 │ 
 460 │ .. function:: my_wait(retry_state)
 461 │ 
 462 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 463 │    :return: number of seconds to wait before next retry
 464 │    :rtype: float
 465 │ 
 466 │ .. function:: my_retry(retry_state)
 467 │ 
 468 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 469 │    :return: whether or not retrying should continue
 470 │    :rtype: bool
 471 │ 
 472 │ .. function:: my_before(retry_state)
 473 │ 
 474 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 475 │ 
 476 │ .. function:: my_after(retry_state)
 477 │ 
 478 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 479 │ 
 480 │ .. function:: my_before_sleep(retry_state)
 481 │ 
 482 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 483 │ 
 484 │ Here's an example with a custom ``before_sleep`` function:
 485 │ 
 486 │ .. testcode::
 487 │ 
 488 │     import logging
 489 │ 
 490 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 491 │ 
 492 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 493 │ 
 494 │     def my_before_sleep(retry_state):
 495 │         if retry_state.attempt_number < 1:
 496 │             loglevel = logging.INFO
 497 │         else:
 498 │             loglevel = logging.WARNING
 499 │         logger.log(
 500 │             loglevel, 'Retrying %s: attempt %s ended with: %s',
 501 │             retry_state.fn, retry_state.attempt_number, retry_state.outcome)
 502 │ 
 503 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before_sleep=my_before_sleep)
 504 │     def raise_my_exception():
 505 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 506 │ 
 507 │     try:
 508 │         raise_my_exception()
 509 │     except RetryError:
 510 │         pass

 513 │ Common Patterns
 514 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 515 │ 
 516 │ **Running setup code between retries** (e.g. reconnecting):
 517 │ 
 518 │ .. testcode::
 519 │ 
 520 │     def reconnect(retry_state):
 521 │         print("Reconnecting before next attempt...")
 522 │ 
 523 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before_sleep=reconnect)
 524 │     def send_data():
 525 │         raise MyException("connection lost")
 526 │ 
 527 │     try:
 528 │         send_data()
 529 │     except RetryError:
 530 │         pass
 531 │ 
 532 │ .. testoutput::
 533 │    :hide:
 534 │ 
 535 │    ...
 536 │ 
 537 │ The ``before_sleep`` callback runs after a failed attempt and before sleeping,
 538 │ making it ideal for re-establishing connections, refreshing tokens, or any
 539 │ other setup that needs to happen before the next attempt.
 540 │ 
 541 │ **Accessing the attempt number inside the function** using the iterator API:
 542 │ 
 543 │ .. testcode::
 544 │ 
 545 │     from tenacity import Retrying
 546 │ 
 547 │     for attempt in Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 548 │         with attempt:
 549 │             print(f"Attempt {attempt.retry_state.attempt_number}")
 550 │             if attempt.retry_state.attempt_number < 3:
 551 │                 raise MyException("not yet")

 554 │    :hide:

 559 │ Changing Arguments at Run Time
 560 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 561 │ 
 562 │ You can change the arguments of a retry decorator as needed when calling it by
 563 │ using the `retry_with` function attached to the wrapped function:
 564 │ 
 565 │ .. testcode::
 566 │ 
 567 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 568 │     def raise_my_exception():
 569 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 570 │ 
 571 │     try:
 572 │         raise_my_exception.retry_with(stop=stop_after_attempt(4))()
 573 │     except Exception:
 574 │         pass
 575 │ 
 576 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)
 577 │ 
 578 │ .. testoutput::
 579 │    :hide:
 580 │ 
 581 │    ...
 582 │ 
 583 │ If you want to use variables to set up the retry parameters, you don't have
 584 │ to use the `retry` decorator - you can instead use `Retrying` directly:
 585 │ 
 586 │ .. testcode::
 587 │ 
 588 │     def never_good_enough(arg1):
 589 │         raise Exception('Invalid argument: {}'.format(arg1))
 590 │ 
 591 │     def try_never_good_enough(max_attempts=3):
 592 │         retryer = Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(max_attempts), reraise=True)
 593 │         retryer(never_good_enough, 'I really do try')
 594 │ 
 595 │ You may also want to change the behaviour of a decorated function temporarily,
 596 │ like in tests to avoid unnecessary wait times. You can modify/patch the `retry`
 597 │ attribute attached to the function. Bear in mind this is a write-only attribute,
 598 │ statistics should be read from the function `statistics` attribute.
 599 │ 
 600 │ .. testcode::
 601 │ 
 602 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_fixed(3))
 603 │     def raise_my_exception():
 604 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 605 │ 
 606 │     from unittest import mock
 607 │ 
 608 │     with mock.patch.object(raise_my_exception.retry, "wait", wait_fixed(0)):
 609 │         try:
 610 │             raise_my_exception()
 611 │         except Exception:
 612 │             pass
 613 │ 
 614 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)
 615 │

 617 │    :hide:

 619 │    ...

 621 │ Disabling Retries
 622 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 623 │ 
 624 │ You can disable retrying entirely by passing ``enabled=False``. When disabled,
 625 │ the decorated function is called directly without any retry logic. This is
 626 │ useful during development or testing when you want fast feedback on failures:
 627 │ 
 628 │ .. testcode::
 629 │ 
 630 │     import os
 631 │ 
 632 │     @retry(
 633 │         enabled=os.getenv("ENABLE_RETRIES", "1") != "0",
 634 │         stop=stop_after_attempt(5),
 635 │         wait=wait_fixed(1),
 636 │     )
 637 │     def call_api():
 638 │         pass  # your code here
 639 │ 
 640 │     call_api()
 641 │ 
 642 │ You can also use ``retry_with`` to disable retries on a per-call basis:
 643 │ 
 644 │ .. testcode::
 645 │ 
 646 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5))
 647 │     def call_api():
 648 │         pass  # your code here
 649 │ 
 650 │     # In tests:
 651 │     call_api.retry_with(enabled=False)()
 652 │ 
 653 │ Retrying code block
 654 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 655 │ 
 656 │ Tenacity allows you to retry a code block without the need to wraps it in an
 657 │ isolated function. This makes it easy to isolate failing block while sharing
 658 │ context. The trick is to combine a for loop and a context manager.
 659 │ 
 660 │ .. testcode::
 661 │ 
 662 │    from tenacity import Retrying, RetryError, stop_after_attempt
 663 │ 
 664 │    try:
 665 │        for attempt in Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 666 │            with attempt:
 667 │                raise Exception('My code is failing!')
 668 │    except RetryError:
 669 │        pass
 670 │ 
 671 │ You can configure every details of retry policy by configuring the Retrying
 672 │ object.
 673 │ 
 674 │ With async code you can use AsyncRetrying.
 675 │ 
 676 │ .. testcode::
 677 │ 
 678 │    from tenacity import AsyncRetrying, RetryError, stop_after_attempt
 679 │ 
 680 │    async def function():
 681 │       try:
 682 │           async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 683 │               with attempt:
 684 │                   raise Exception('My code is failing!')
 685 │       except RetryError:
 686 │           pass
 687 │ 
 688 │ In both cases, you may want to set the result to the attempt so it's available
 689 │ in retry strategies like ``retry_if_result``. This can be done accessing the
 690 │ ``retry_state`` property:
 691 │ 
 692 │ .. testcode::
 693 │ 
 694 │     from tenacity import AsyncRetrying, retry_if_result
 695 │ 
 696 │     async def function():
 697 │        async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(retry=retry_if_result(lambda x: x < 3)):
 698 │            with attempt:
 699 │                result = 1  # Some complex calculation, function call, etc.
 700 │            if not attempt.retry_state.outcome.failed:
 701 │                attempt.retry_state.set_result(result)
 702 │        return result
 703 │ 
 704 │ Async and retry
 705 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 706 │ 
 707 │ Finally, ``retry`` works also on asyncio, Trio, and Tornado coroutines.
 708 │ Sleeps are done asynchronously too.
 709 │ 
 710 │ .. code-block:: python
 711 │ 
 712 │     @retry
 713 │     async def my_asyncio_function():
 714 │         await asyncio.getaddrinfo('8.8.8.8', 53)
 715 │ 
 716 │ .. code-block:: python
 717 │ 
 718 │     @retry
 719 │     async def my_async_trio_function():
 720 │         await trio.socket.getaddrinfo('8.8.8.8', 53)
 721 │ 
 722 │ .. code-block:: python
 723 │ 
 724 │     @retry
 725 │     async def my_async_tornado_function(http_client, url):
 726 │         await http_client.fetch(url)
 727 │ 
 728 │ You can use alternative event loops by passing the correct sleep function:
 729 │ 
 730 │ .. code-block:: python
 731 │ 
 732 │     @retry(sleep=trio.sleep)
 733 │     async def my_async_trio_function_with_sleep():
 734 │         ...

  18 │ Tenacity is an Apache 2.0 licensed general-purpose retrying library, written in
  19 │ Python, to simplify the task of adding retry behavior to just about anything.
  20 │ It originates from `a fork of retrying

  22 │ `maintained <https://julien.danjou.info/python-tenacity/>`_. Tenacity isn't

  79 │ Examples

  82 │ Basic Retry
  83 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~
  84 │ 
  85 │ .. testsetup::
  86 │ 
  87 │     import logging
  88 │     #
  89 │     # Note the following import is used for demonstration convenience only.
  90 │     # Production code should always explicitly import the names it needs.
  91 │     #
  92 │     from tenacity import *
  93 │ 
  94 │     class MyException(Exception):
  95 │         pass
  96 │ 
  97 │ As you saw above, the default behavior is to retry forever without waiting when
  98 │ an exception is raised.
  99 │ 
 100 │ .. testcode::
 101 │ 
 102 │     @retry
 103 │     def never_gonna_give_you_up():
 104 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions, don't wait between retries")
 105 │         raise Exception
 106 │ 
 107 │ Stopping
 108 │ ~~~~~~~~
 109 │ 
 110 │ Let's be a little less persistent and set some boundaries, such as the number
 111 │ of attempts before giving up.
 112 │ 
 113 │ .. testcode::
 114 │ 
 115 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(7))
 116 │     def stop_after_7_attempts():
 117 │         print("Stopping after 7 attempts")
 118 │         raise Exception
 119 │ 
 120 │ We don't have all day, so let's set a boundary for how long we should be
 121 │ retrying stuff.
 122 │ 
 123 │ .. testcode::
 124 │ 
 125 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_delay(10))
 126 │     def stop_after_10_s():
 127 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds")
 128 │         raise Exception
 129 │ 
 130 │ If you're on a tight deadline, and exceeding your delay time isn't ok,
 131 │ then you can give up on retries one attempt before you would exceed the delay.
 132 │ 
 133 │ .. testcode::
 134 │ 
 135 │     @retry(stop=stop_before_delay(10))
 136 │     def stop_before_10_s():
 137 │         print("Stopping 1 attempt before 10 seconds")
 138 │         raise Exception
 139 │ 
 140 │ You can combine several stop conditions by using the `|` operator:
 141 │ 
 142 │ .. testcode::
 143 │ 
 144 │     @retry(stop=(stop_after_delay(10) | stop_after_attempt(5)))
 145 │     def stop_after_10_s_or_5_retries():
 146 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds or 5 retries")
 147 │         raise Exception
 148 │ 
 149 │ Waiting before retrying
 150 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 151 │ 
 152 │ Most things don't like to be polled as fast as possible, so let's just wait 2
 153 │ seconds between retries.
 154 │ 
 155 │ .. testcode::
 156 │ 
 157 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(2))
 158 │     def wait_2_s():
 159 │         print("Wait 2 second between retries")
 160 │         raise Exception
 161 │ 
 162 │ Some things perform best with a bit of randomness injected.
 163 │ 
 164 │ .. testcode::
 165 │ 
 166 │     @retry(wait=wait_random(min=1, max=2))
 167 │     def wait_random_1_to_2_s():
 168 │         print("Randomly wait 1 to 2 seconds between retries")
 169 │         raise Exception
 170 │ 
 171 │ Then again, it's hard to beat exponential backoff when retrying distributed
 172 │ services and other remote endpoints.
 173 │ 
 174 │ .. testcode::
 175 │ 
 176 │     @retry(wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=4, max=10))
 177 │     def wait_exponential_1():
 178 │         print("Wait 2^x * 1 second between each retry starting with 4 seconds, then up to 10 seconds, then 10 seconds afterwards")
 179 │         raise Exception
 180 │ 
 181 │ 
 182 │ Then again, it's also hard to beat combining fixed waits and jitter (to
 183 │ help avoid thundering herds) when retrying distributed services and other
 184 │ remote endpoints.
 185 │ 
 186 │ .. testcode::
 187 │ 
 188 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(3) + wait_random(0, 2))
 189 │     def wait_fixed_jitter():
 190 │         print("Wait at least 3 seconds, and add up to 2 seconds of random delay")
 191 │         raise Exception
 192 │ 
 193 │ When multiple processes are in contention for a shared resource, exponentially
 194 │ increasing jitter helps minimise collisions.
 195 │ 
 196 │ .. testcode::
 197 │ 
 198 │     @retry(wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=1, max=60))
 199 │     def wait_exponential_jitter():
 200 │         print("Randomly wait up to 2^x * 1 seconds between each retry until the range reaches 60 seconds, then randomly up to 60 seconds afterwards")
 201 │         raise Exception
 202 │ 
 203 │ 
 204 │ Sometimes it's necessary to build a chain of backoffs.
 205 │ 
 206 │ .. testcode::
 207 │ 
 208 │     @retry(wait=wait_chain(*[wait_fixed(3) for i in range(3)] +
 209 │                            [wait_fixed(7) for i in range(2)] +
 210 │                            [wait_fixed(9)]))
 211 │     def wait_fixed_chained():
 212 │         print("Wait 3s for 3 attempts, 7s for the next 2 attempts and 9s for all attempts thereafter")
 213 │         raise Exception

 215 │ Whether to retry
 216 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 217 │ 
 218 │ We have a few options for dealing with retries that raise specific or general
 219 │ exceptions, as in the cases here.
 220 │ 
 221 │ .. testcode::
 222 │ 
 223 │     class ClientError(Exception):
 224 │         """Some type of client error."""
 225 │ 
 226 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(IOError))
 227 │     def might_io_error():
 228 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if an IOError occurs, raise any other errors")
 229 │         raise Exception
 230 │ 
 231 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_not_exception_type(ClientError))
 232 │     def might_client_error():
 233 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if any error other than ClientError occurs. Immediately raise ClientError.")
 234 │         raise Exception
 235 │ 
 236 │ We can also use the result of the function to alter the behavior of retrying.
 237 │ 
 238 │ .. testcode::
 239 │ 
 240 │     def is_none_p(value):
 241 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 242 │         return value is None
 243 │ 
 244 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_result(is_none_p))
 245 │     def might_return_none():
 246 │         print("Retry with no wait if return value is None")
 247 │ 
 248 │ See also these methods:
 249 │ 
 250 │ .. testcode::
 251 │ 
 252 │     retry_if_exception
 253 │     retry_if_exception_type
 254 │     retry_if_not_exception_type
 255 │     retry_unless_exception_type
 256 │     retry_if_result
 257 │     retry_if_not_result
 258 │     retry_if_exception_message
 259 │     retry_if_not_exception_message
 260 │     retry_any
 261 │     retry_all
 262 │ 
 263 │ We can also combine several conditions:
 264 │ 
 265 │ .. testcode::
 266 │ 
 267 │     def is_none_p(value):
 268 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 269 │         return value is None
 270 │ 
 271 │     @retry(retry=(retry_if_result(is_none_p) | retry_if_exception_type()))
 272 │     def might_return_none():
 273 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions with no wait if return value is None")
 274 │ 
 275 │ Any combination of stop, wait, etc. is also supported to give you the freedom
 276 │ to mix and match.
 277 │ 
 278 │ It's also possible to retry explicitly at any time by raising the `TryAgain`
 279 │ exception:
 280 │ 
 281 │ .. testcode::
 282 │ 
 283 │    @retry
 284 │    def do_something():
 285 │        result = something_else()
 286 │        if result == 23:
 287 │           raise TryAgain

 289 │ Error Handling
 290 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 291 │ 
 292 │ Normally when your function fails its final time (and will not be retried again based on your settings),
 293 │ a `RetryError` is raised. The exception your code encountered will be shown somewhere in the *middle*
 294 │ of the stack trace.
 295 │ 
 296 │ If you would rather see the exception your code encountered at the *end* of the stack trace (where it
 297 │ is most visible), you can set `reraise=True`.
 298 │ 
 299 │ .. testcode::
 300 │ 
 301 │     @retry(reraise=True, stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 302 │     def raise_my_exception():
 303 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 304 │ 
 305 │     try:
 306 │         raise_my_exception()
 307 │     except MyException:
 308 │         # timed out retrying
 309 │         pass

 311 │ Before and After Retry, and Logging
 312 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 313 │ 
 314 │ It's possible to execute an action before any attempt of calling the function
 315 │ by using the before callback function:
 316 │ 
 317 │ .. testcode::
 318 │ 
 319 │     import logging
 320 │     import sys
 321 │ 
 322 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 323 │ 
 324 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 325 │ 
 326 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before=before_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 327 │     def raise_my_exception():
 328 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 329 │ 
 330 │ In the same spirit, It's possible to execute after a call that failed:
 331 │ 
 332 │ .. testcode::
 333 │ 
 334 │     import logging
 335 │     import sys
 336 │ 
 337 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 338 │ 
 339 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 340 │ 
 341 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=after_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 342 │     def raise_my_exception():
 343 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 344 │ 
 345 │ It's also possible to only log failures that are going to be retried. Normally
 346 │ retries happen after a wait interval, so the keyword argument is called
 347 │ ``before_sleep``:
 348 │ 
 349 │ .. testcode::
 350 │ 
 351 │     import logging
 352 │     import sys
 353 │ 
 354 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 355 │ 
 356 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 357 │ 
 358 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 359 │            before_sleep=before_sleep_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 360 │     def raise_my_exception():
 361 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 362 │

 388 │ Custom Callbacks
 389 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 390 │ 
 391 │ You can also define your own callbacks. The callback should accept one
 392 │ parameter called ``retry_state`` that contains all information about current
 393 │ retry invocation.
 394 │ 
 395 │ For example, you can call a custom callback function after all retries failed,
 396 │ without raising an exception (or you can re-raise or do anything really)
 397 │ 
 398 │ .. testcode::
 399 │ 
 400 │     def return_last_value(retry_state):
 401 │         """return the result of the last call attempt"""
 402 │         return retry_state.outcome.result()
 403 │ 
 404 │     def is_false(value):
 405 │         """Return True if value is False"""
 406 │         return value is False
 407 │ 
 408 │     # will return False after trying 3 times to get a different result
 409 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 410 │            retry_error_callback=return_last_value,
 411 │            retry=retry_if_result(is_false))
 412 │     def eventually_return_false():
 413 │         return False
 414 │ 
 415 │ RetryCallState
 416 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 417 │ 
 418 │ ``retry_state`` argument is an object of :class:`~tenacity.RetryCallState` class.
 419 │ Its most useful attributes are:
 420 │ 
 421 │ * ``attempt_number`` — number of the current attempt (starts at 1)
 422 │ * ``outcome`` — a :class:`concurrent.futures.Future` holding the last result or exception
 423 │ * ``seconds_since_start`` — total elapsed seconds from the first attempt to the last outcome (``None`` if no outcome yet)
 424 │ * ``idle_for`` — cumulative seconds spent sleeping between attempts
 425 │ * ``start_time`` — :func:`time.monotonic` timestamp of the first attempt
 426 │ 
 427 │ For example, to log the total elapsed time after all retries:
 428 │ 
 429 │ .. testcode::
 430 │ 
 431 │     import logging
 432 │ 
 433 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 434 │ 
 435 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 436 │ 
 437 │     def log_elapsed(retry_state):
 438 │         logger.info('Finished after %.3fs', retry_state.seconds_since_start)
 439 │ 
 440 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=log_elapsed)
 441 │     def raise_my_exception():
 442 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 443 │ 
 444 │     try:
 445 │         raise_my_exception()
 446 │     except RetryError:
 447 │         pass
 448 │ 
 449 │ Other Custom Callbacks
 450 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 451 │ 
 452 │ It's also possible to define custom callbacks for other keyword arguments.
 453 │ 
 454 │ .. function:: my_stop(retry_state)
 455 │ 
 456 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 457 │    :return: whether or not retrying should stop
 458 │    :rtype: bool
 459 │ 
 460 │ .. function:: my_wait(retry_state)
 461 │ 
 462 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 463 │    :return: number of seconds to wait before next retry
 464 │    :rtype: float
 465 │ 
 466 │ .. function:: my_retry(retry_state)
 467 │ 
 468 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 469 │    :return: whether or not retrying should continue
 470 │    :rtype: bool
 471 │ 
 472 │ .. function:: my_before(retry_state)
 473 │ 
 474 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 475 │ 
 476 │ .. function:: my_after(retry_state)
 477 │ 
 478 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 479 │ 
 480 │ .. function:: my_before_sleep(retry_state)
 481 │ 
 482 │    :param RetryCallState retry_state: info about current retry invocation
 483 │ 
 484 │ Here's an example with a custom ``before_sleep`` function:
 485 │ 
 486 │ .. testcode::
 487 │ 
 488 │     import logging
 489 │ 
 490 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 491 │ 
 492 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 493 │ 
 494 │     def my_before_sleep(retry_state):
 495 │         if retry_state.attempt_number < 1:
 496 │             loglevel = logging.INFO
 497 │         else:
 498 │             loglevel = logging.WARNING
 499 │         logger.log(
 500 │             loglevel, 'Retrying %s: attempt %s ended with: %s',
 501 │             retry_state.fn, retry_state.attempt_number, retry_state.outcome)
 502 │ 
 503 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before_sleep=my_before_sleep)
 504 │     def raise_my_exception():
 505 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 506 │ 
 507 │     try:
 508 │         raise_my_exception()
 509 │     except RetryError:
 510 │         pass
 511 │

 513 │ Common Patterns
 514 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 515 │ 
 516 │ **Running setup code between retries** (e.g. reconnecting):
 517 │ 
 518 │ .. testcode::
 519 │ 
 520 │     def reconnect(retry_state):
 521 │         print("Reconnecting before next attempt...")
 522 │ 
 523 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before_sleep=reconnect)
 524 │     def send_data():
 525 │         raise MyException("connection lost")
 526 │ 
 527 │     try:
 528 │         send_data()
 529 │     except RetryError:
 530 │         pass
 531 │

 533 │    :hide:
 534 │ 
 535 │    ...
 536 │ 
 537 │ The ``before_sleep`` callback runs after a failed attempt and before sleeping,
 538 │ making it ideal for re-establishing connections, refreshing tokens, or any
 539 │ other setup that needs to happen before the next attempt.
 540 │ 
 541 │ **Accessing the attempt number inside the function** using the iterator API:
 542 │ 
 543 │ .. testcode::
 544 │ 
 545 │     from tenacity import Retrying
 546 │ 
 547 │     for attempt in Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 548 │         with attempt:
 549 │             print(f"Attempt {attempt.retry_state.attempt_number}")
 550 │             if attempt.retry_state.attempt_number < 3:
 551 │                 raise MyException("not yet")

 559 │ Changing Arguments at Run Time
 560 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 561 │ 
 562 │ You can change the arguments of a retry decorator as needed when calling it by
 563 │ using the `retry_with` function attached to the wrapped function:
 564 │ 
 565 │ .. testcode::
 566 │ 
 567 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 568 │     def raise_my_exception():
 569 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 570 │ 
 571 │     try:
 572 │         raise_my_exception.retry_with(stop=stop_after_attempt(4))()
 573 │     except Exception:
 574 │         pass
 575 │ 
 576 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)
 577 │

 579 │    :hide:
 580 │ 
 581 │    ...
 582 │ 
 583 │ If you want to use variables to set up the retry parameters, you don't have
 584 │ to use the `retry` decorator - you can instead use `Retrying` directly:
 585 │ 
 586 │ .. testcode::
 587 │ 
 588 │     def never_good_enough(arg1):
 589 │         raise Exception('Invalid argument: {}'.format(arg1))
 590 │ 
 591 │     def try_never_good_enough(max_attempts=3):
 592 │         retryer = Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(max_attempts), reraise=True)
 593 │         retryer(never_good_enough, 'I really do try')
 594 │ 
 595 │ You may also want to change the behaviour of a decorated function temporarily,
 596 │ like in tests to avoid unnecessary wait times. You can modify/patch the `retry`
 597 │ attribute attached to the function. Bear in mind this is a write-only attribute,
 598 │ statistics should be read from the function `statistics` attribute.
 599 │ 
 600 │ .. testcode::
 601 │ 
 602 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), wait=wait_fixed(3))
 603 │     def raise_my_exception():
 604 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 605 │ 
 606 │     from unittest import mock
 607 │ 
 608 │     with mock.patch.object(raise_my_exception.retry, "wait", wait_fixed(0)):
 609 │         try:
 610 │             raise_my_exception()
 611 │         except Exception:
 612 │             pass
 613 │ 
 614 │     print(raise_my_exception.statistics)

 621 │ Disabling Retries
 622 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 623 │ 
 624 │ You can disable retrying entirely by passing ``enabled=False``. When disabled,
 625 │ the decorated function is called directly without any retry logic. This is
 626 │ useful during development or testing when you want fast feedback on failures:
 627 │ 
 628 │ .. testcode::
 629 │ 
 630 │     import os
 631 │ 
 632 │     @retry(
 633 │         enabled=os.getenv("ENABLE_RETRIES", "1") != "0",
 634 │         stop=stop_after_attempt(5),
 635 │         wait=wait_fixed(1),
 636 │     )
 637 │     def call_api():
 638 │         pass  # your code here
 639 │ 
 640 │     call_api()
 641 │ 
 642 │ You can also use ``retry_with`` to disable retries on a per-call basis:
 643 │ 
 644 │ .. testcode::
 645 │ 
 646 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5))
 647 │     def call_api():
 648 │         pass  # your code here
 649 │ 
 650 │     # In tests:
 651 │     call_api.retry_with(enabled=False)()
 652 │ 
 653 │ Retrying code block
 654 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 655 │ 
 656 │ Tenacity allows you to retry a code block without the need to wraps it in an
 657 │ isolated function. This makes it easy to isolate failing block while sharing
 658 │ context. The trick is to combine a for loop and a context manager.
 659 │ 
 660 │ .. testcode::
 661 │ 
 662 │    from tenacity import Retrying, RetryError, stop_after_attempt
 663 │ 
 664 │    try:
 665 │        for attempt in Retrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 666 │            with attempt:
 667 │                raise Exception('My code is failing!')
 668 │    except RetryError:
 669 │        pass
 670 │ 
 671 │ You can configure every details of retry policy by configuring the Retrying
 672 │ object.
 673 │ 
 674 │ With async code you can use AsyncRetrying.
 675 │ 
 676 │ .. testcode::
 677 │ 
 678 │    from tenacity import AsyncRetrying, RetryError, stop_after_attempt
 679 │ 
 680 │    async def function():
 681 │       try:
 682 │           async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(stop=stop_after_attempt(3)):
 683 │               with attempt:
 684 │                   raise Exception('My code is failing!')
 685 │       except RetryError:
 686 │           pass
 687 │ 
 688 │ In both cases, you may want to set the result to the attempt so it's available
 689 │ in retry strategies like ``retry_if_result``. This can be done accessing the
 690 │ ``retry_state`` property:
 691 │ 
 692 │ .. testcode::
 693 │ 
 694 │     from tenacity import AsyncRetrying, retry_if_result
 695 │ 
 696 │     async def function():
 697 │        async for attempt in AsyncRetrying(retry=retry_if_result(lambda x: x < 3)):
 698 │            with attempt:
 699 │                result = 1  # Some complex calculation, function call, etc.
 700 │            if not attempt.retry_state.outcome.failed:
 701 │                attempt.retry_state.set_result(result)
 702 │        return result

 704 │ Async and retry
 705 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 706 │ 
 707 │ Finally, ``retry`` works also on asyncio, Trio, and Tornado coroutines.
 708 │ Sleeps are done asynchronously too.
 709 │ 
 710 │ .. code-block:: python
 711 │ 
 712 │     @retry
 713 │     async def my_asyncio_function():
 714 │         await asyncio.getaddrinfo('8.8.8.8', 53)
 715 │ 
 716 │ .. code-block:: python
 717 │ 
 718 │     @retry
 719 │     async def my_async_trio_function():
 720 │         await trio.socket.getaddrinfo('8.8.8.8', 53)
 721 │ 
 722 │ .. code-block:: python
 723 │ 
 724 │     @retry
 725 │     async def my_async_tornado_function(http_client, url):
 726 │         await http_client.fetch(url)

  79 │ Examples
  80 │ ----------
  81 │ 
  82 │ Basic Retry
  83 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~
  84 │ 
  85 │ .. testsetup::
  86 │ 
  87 │     import logging
  88 │     #
  89 │     # Note the following import is used for demonstration convenience only.
  90 │     # Production code should always explicitly import the names it needs.
  91 │     #
  92 │     from tenacity import *
  93 │ 
  94 │     class MyException(Exception):
  95 │         pass
  96 │ 
  97 │ As you saw above, the default behavior is to retry forever without waiting when
  98 │ an exception is raised.
  99 │ 
 100 │ .. testcode::
 101 │ 
 102 │     @retry
 103 │     def never_gonna_give_you_up():
 104 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions, don't wait between retries")
 105 │         raise Exception
 106 │ 
 107 │ Stopping
 108 │ ~~~~~~~~
 109 │ 
 110 │ Let's be a little less persistent and set some boundaries, such as the number
 111 │ of attempts before giving up.
 112 │ 
 113 │ .. testcode::
 114 │ 
 115 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(7))
 116 │     def stop_after_7_attempts():
 117 │         print("Stopping after 7 attempts")
 118 │         raise Exception
 119 │ 
 120 │ We don't have all day, so let's set a boundary for how long we should be
 121 │ retrying stuff.
 122 │ 
 123 │ .. testcode::
 124 │ 
 125 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_delay(10))
 126 │     def stop_after_10_s():
 127 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds")
 128 │         raise Exception
 129 │ 
 130 │ If you're on a tight deadline, and exceeding your delay time isn't ok,
 131 │ then you can give up on retries one attempt before you would exceed the delay.
 132 │ 
 133 │ .. testcode::
 134 │ 
 135 │     @retry(stop=stop_before_delay(10))
 136 │     def stop_before_10_s():
 137 │         print("Stopping 1 attempt before 10 seconds")
 138 │         raise Exception
 139 │ 
 140 │ You can combine several stop conditions by using the `|` operator:
 141 │ 
 142 │ .. testcode::
 143 │ 
 144 │     @retry(stop=(stop_after_delay(10) | stop_after_attempt(5)))
 145 │     def stop_after_10_s_or_5_retries():
 146 │         print("Stopping after 10 seconds or 5 retries")
 147 │         raise Exception
 148 │ 
 149 │ Waiting before retrying
 150 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 151 │ 
 152 │ Most things don't like to be polled as fast as possible, so let's just wait 2
 153 │ seconds between retries.
 154 │ 
 155 │ .. testcode::
 156 │ 
 157 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(2))
 158 │     def wait_2_s():
 159 │         print("Wait 2 second between retries")
 160 │         raise Exception
 161 │ 
 162 │ Some things perform best with a bit of randomness injected.
 163 │ 
 164 │ .. testcode::
 165 │ 
 166 │     @retry(wait=wait_random(min=1, max=2))
 167 │     def wait_random_1_to_2_s():
 168 │         print("Randomly wait 1 to 2 seconds between retries")
 169 │         raise Exception
 170 │ 
 171 │ Then again, it's hard to beat exponential backoff when retrying distributed
 172 │ services and other remote endpoints.
 173 │ 
 174 │ .. testcode::
 175 │ 
 176 │     @retry(wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=4, max=10))
 177 │     def wait_exponential_1():
 178 │         print("Wait 2^x * 1 second between each retry starting with 4 seconds, then up to 10 seconds, then 10 seconds afterwards")
 179 │         raise Exception
 180 │ 
 181 │ 
 182 │ Then again, it's also hard to beat combining fixed waits and jitter (to
 183 │ help avoid thundering herds) when retrying distributed services and other
 184 │ remote endpoints.
 185 │ 
 186 │ .. testcode::
 187 │ 
 188 │     @retry(wait=wait_fixed(3) + wait_random(0, 2))
 189 │     def wait_fixed_jitter():
 190 │         print("Wait at least 3 seconds, and add up to 2 seconds of random delay")
 191 │         raise Exception
 192 │ 
 193 │ When multiple processes are in contention for a shared resource, exponentially
 194 │ increasing jitter helps minimise collisions.
 195 │ 
 196 │ .. testcode::
 197 │ 
 198 │     @retry(wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=1, max=60))
 199 │     def wait_exponential_jitter():
 200 │         print("Randomly wait up to 2^x * 1 seconds between each retry until the range reaches 60 seconds, then randomly up to 60 seconds afterwards")
 201 │         raise Exception
 202 │ 
 203 │ 
 204 │ Sometimes it's necessary to build a chain of backoffs.
 205 │ 
 206 │ .. testcode::
 207 │ 
 208 │     @retry(wait=wait_chain(*[wait_fixed(3) for i in range(3)] +
 209 │                            [wait_fixed(7) for i in range(2)] +
 210 │                            [wait_fixed(9)]))
 211 │     def wait_fixed_chained():
 212 │         print("Wait 3s for 3 attempts, 7s for the next 2 attempts and 9s for all attempts thereafter")
 213 │         raise Exception
 214 │ 
 215 │ Whether to retry
 216 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 217 │ 
 218 │ We have a few options for dealing with retries that raise specific or general
 219 │ exceptions, as in the cases here.
 220 │ 
 221 │ .. testcode::
 222 │ 
 223 │     class ClientError(Exception):
 224 │         """Some type of client error."""
 225 │ 
 226 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(IOError))
 227 │     def might_io_error():
 228 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if an IOError occurs, raise any other errors")
 229 │         raise Exception
 230 │ 
 231 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_not_exception_type(ClientError))
 232 │     def might_client_error():
 233 │         print("Retry forever with no wait if any error other than ClientError occurs. Immediately raise ClientError.")
 234 │         raise Exception
 235 │ 
 236 │ We can also use the result of the function to alter the behavior of retrying.
 237 │ 
 238 │ .. testcode::
 239 │ 
 240 │     def is_none_p(value):
 241 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 242 │         return value is None
 243 │ 
 244 │     @retry(retry=retry_if_result(is_none_p))
 245 │     def might_return_none():
 246 │         print("Retry with no wait if return value is None")
 247 │ 
 248 │ See also these methods:
 249 │ 
 250 │ .. testcode::
 251 │ 
 252 │     retry_if_exception
 253 │     retry_if_exception_type
 254 │     retry_if_not_exception_type
 255 │     retry_unless_exception_type
 256 │     retry_if_result
 257 │     retry_if_not_result
 258 │     retry_if_exception_message
 259 │     retry_if_not_exception_message
 260 │     retry_any
 261 │     retry_all
 262 │ 
 263 │ We can also combine several conditions:
 264 │ 
 265 │ .. testcode::
 266 │ 
 267 │     def is_none_p(value):
 268 │         """Return True if value is None"""
 269 │         return value is None
 270 │ 
 271 │     @retry(retry=(retry_if_result(is_none_p) | retry_if_exception_type()))
 272 │     def might_return_none():
 273 │         print("Retry forever ignoring Exceptions with no wait if return value is None")
 274 │ 
 275 │ Any combination of stop, wait, etc. is also supported to give you the freedom
 276 │ to mix and match.
 277 │ 
 278 │ It's also possible to retry explicitly at any time by raising the `TryAgain`
 279 │ exception:
 280 │ 
 281 │ .. testcode::
 282 │ 
 283 │    @retry
 284 │    def do_something():
 285 │        result = something_else()
 286 │        if result == 23:
 287 │           raise TryAgain
 288 │ 
 289 │ Error Handling
 290 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 291 │ 
 292 │ Normally when your function fails its final time (and will not be retried again based on your settings),
 293 │ a `RetryError` is raised. The exception your code encountered will be shown somewhere in the *middle*
 294 │ of the stack trace.
 295 │ 
 296 │ If you would rather see the exception your code encountered at the *end* of the stack trace (where it
 297 │ is most visible), you can set `reraise=True`.
 298 │ 
 299 │ .. testcode::
 300 │ 
 301 │     @retry(reraise=True, stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
 302 │     def raise_my_exception():
 303 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 304 │ 
 305 │     try:
 306 │         raise_my_exception()
 307 │     except MyException:
 308 │         # timed out retrying
 309 │         pass
 310 │ 
 311 │ Before and After Retry, and Logging
 312 │ ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 313 │ 
 314 │ It's possible to execute an action before any attempt of calling the function
 315 │ by using the before callback function:
 316 │ 
 317 │ .. testcode::
 318 │ 
 319 │     import logging
 320 │     import sys
 321 │ 
 322 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 323 │ 
 324 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 325 │ 
 326 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), before=before_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 327 │     def raise_my_exception():
 328 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 329 │ 
 330 │ In the same spirit, It's possible to execute after a call that failed:
 331 │ 
 332 │ .. testcode::
 333 │ 
 334 │     import logging
 335 │     import sys
 336 │ 
 337 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 338 │ 
 339 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 340 │ 
 341 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3), after=after_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 342 │     def raise_my_exception():
 343 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 344 │ 
 345 │ It's also possible to only log failures that are going to be retried. Normally
 346 │ retries happen after a wait interval, so the keyword argument is called
 347 │ ``before_sleep``:
 348 │ 
 349 │ .. testcode::
 350 │ 
 351 │     import logging
 352 │     import sys
 353 │ 
 354 │     logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stderr, level=logging.DEBUG)
 355 │ 
 356 │     logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
 357 │ 
 358 │     @retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
 359 │            before_sleep=before_sleep_log(logger, logging.DEBUG))
 360 │     def raise_my_exception():
 361 │         raise MyException("Fail")
 362 │

 365 │ ~~~~~~~~~~

 373 │     def raise_my_exception():
